title: Heap: Push and Pop
oneLiner: A binary heap IS a binary tree -- same shape as a BST, but the invariant is different: every parent is smaller (or bigger) than its children, not ordered left/right.
keyTakeaway: A heap only guarantees ONE thing: every parent is <= (min-heap) or >= (max-heap) its children -- unlike a BST, there's no left/right ordering rule, so a value could legally be on either side. That weaker invariant is exactly what makes push/pop O(log n) with a much simpler operation than a BST's: always insert/remove at the END (the next open array slot, keeping the tree perfectly complete), then "bubble" the disturbance up or down until the heap property holds again.
explanation: A binary heap is stored exactly like the trees in this app already are -- a level-order array, parent at i, children at 2i+1/2i+2 -- which is no accident, it's the standard way to implement one, since a heap is always a COMPLETE tree (every level full except possibly the last, filled left to right), so array positions never have gaps to represent. PUSH: append the new value at the next open slot (keeps the tree complete), then "sift up" -- while it's smaller than its parent (min-heap), swap with the parent and repeat. POP: the minimum is always the root (that's the whole point of the invariant), so save it, move the LAST element into the root position (keeps the tree complete again), shrink by one slot, then "sift down" -- while it's bigger than its smallest child, swap with that child and repeat. This lesson encodes a sequence of operations as one array, same trick Queues used: a positive value means push(value), and 0 means pop (remove and record the current minimum). Watch out for sifting down against the WRONG child -- you must compare against the SMALLER of the two children, not just the left one, or the heap property can end up violated on the side you didn't check.

recognitionSignals: You repeatedly need "the current smallest/largest" out of a changing collection -- not a one-time sort, a running priority.
The problem mentions "top K," "kth largest/smallest," "priority," or a scheduler-like "always process the most urgent thing next."
gotchas: Sifting down must compare against the SMALLER of the two children (min-heap), not just the left one -- comparing only one side can leave the heap property broken on the other.
Both push and pop must keep the tree COMPLETE (no gaps) -- push always appends at the end, pop always pulls the LAST element up to fill the root's old spot, never leaving a hole in the middle.
A heap only guarantees the ROOT is the min -- nothing about the relative order of any two sibling or cousin nodes. Don't assume a heap is "mostly sorted"; only the very top is guaranteed.
confusableWith: Binary Search Trees: Insert (this track) looks similar (a tree, comparisons while walking down) but enforces a completely different invariant (left < node <= right vs. parent <= children) and, unlike a heap, is NOT always kept complete/balanced by plain insertion.

complexity.note: ProcessHeapOps runs m operations. Each push or pop sifts along one root-to-leaf path of a complete tree, and a complete tree with n nodes has height about log₂ n, where n is the heap's size (never more than m). So the whole run is O(m log n). Space is O(n) for the heap, not counting the output list of popped values; counting the output too, it is O(m).
